### 0. Task setup

```{r task-setup}
library(drosophila2probe)
library(Biostrings)

probes_dss <- DNAStringSet(drosophila2probe)
N <- length(probes_dss)
M <- width(probes_dss)[1]

probes_car <- as.character(probes_dss)
probes_M <- matrix(unlist(strsplit(probes_car, "")), nrow = N)
probes_M[1:10, 1:10]

dim(probes_M) # 265400 DNA probes, all having the length of 25
```

The goal is to compute the GC content of the probes, which are rows of the character matrix.

### 1. For-loops over both rows and columns

```{r for-loop-both-rows-columns}
system.time({
  GC_content <- vector("numeric", N)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    GC_count_i <- 0
    for (j in 1:M) {
      if (probes_M[i, j] == "G" | probes_M[i, j] == "C") {
        GC_count_i <- GC_count_i + 1
      }
    }
    GC_content[i] <- GC_count_i / M
  }
})
```

`system.time()` can report the run time of the program; it took more than 3 seconds to finish the first version of code.

### 2. Vectorization over columns

```{r vectorization-over-columns}
system.time({
  GC_content2 <- vector("numeric", N)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    GC_content2[i] <-
      sum(probes_M[i, ] == "G" | probes_M[i, ] == "C") / M
  }
})
```

The iteration over `j` can be removed by using a trick. We can directly `sum` over the logical vectors to get the count of G and C, since running arithmetic calculation on logical values (`TRUE` and `FALSE`) in R can be treated as `TRUE = 1` and `FALSE = 0`.

By not writing a for-loop over the columns (nucleotide positions), we can already save around 10-fold of time.

### 3. Vectorization over both rows and columns (no for-loop)

```{r vectorization-over-both-rows-columns}
system.time({
  GC_content3 <- rowMeans(probes_M == "G" | probes_M == "C")
})
```

With vectorized code, it took around 0.15 seconds, which is around 50 times faster than the first version of code.

### 4. Use Bioconductor function `letterFrequency()`

```{r bioconductor-letterfrequency}
system.time({
  GC_content4 <- as.vector(letterFrequency(probes_dss, "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
})

# Check if all the codes yield identical results
identical(GC_content, GC_content2, GC_content3, GC_content4)
```

The Bioconductor function is the fastest overall.

## Take-home messages

<mark>Use **vectorized** (multiple-input / multiple-output) functions in R, and always try to avoid using for-loops. Your R code can become extremely inefficient if it contains a for-loop having more than around 10,000 iterations. In addition, before you program something new, always try to search online to see if there are existing functions for your problem.</mark>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<mark>Some commonly used vectorized functions in R: `rowSums()`, `colSums()`, `rowMeans()`, `colMeans()`, `rowVars()`, `rowttests()`, `rowpAUCs()`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `sum()`, `==`.</mark>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Quizzes

Suppose we want to find differentially expressed genes among 20,000 genes between conditions A and B, each having 3 biological replicates. Your task is to realize 2-sample t-tests for each gene, first using a for-loop and then the vectorized way. (I expect you to yield p-value vector of length 20,000)

```{r quiz-simulation-and-dgea}
## Simulate the above mentioned data
set.seed(123)
GeneExpressionMatrix <- matrix(rnorm(20000*6, mean = 2, sd = 1), ncol = 6)
Design <- c("A","A","A","B","B","B")
Indx_Change <- sample.int(20000, 100)
GeneExpressionMatrix[Indx_Change, Design == "B"] <- GeneExpressionMatrix[Indx_Change, Design == "B"] + 1 # Add effect sizes in a subset of genes

## Please write your code bellow:
# Realize DGEA with for-loop
system.time({
pvalues_vec1 <- rep(NA, 20000)
for (i in 1:20000){
 pvalues_vec1[i] <- t.test(GeneExpressionMatrix[i,]~Design)$p.value
}
})

# Realize DGEA with apply()
system.time({
pvalues_vec2 <- apply(GeneExpressionMatrix, 1, function(x) t.test(x ~ Design)$p.value)
})

# Realize DGEA with vectorized function 
system.time({
pvalues_vec3 <- genefilter::rowttests(GeneExpressionMatrix, as.factor(Design))[,3]
})

identical(pvalues_vec1, pvalues_vec2, pvalues_vec3)
```

In the end, evaluate the running times of each coding method with `system.time()`. Is `apply()` faster than a for-loop?

> NO!!!
